title: The song of the flute
hookLine: a flute plays in the forest, and the cows stop chewing and the rivers slow down
carry: empty of ego, so God can play through you
tomorrow: jnana: a seed with nothing inside

cards: A song comes on in a store, or a car, and for three minutes you're not there anymore. You're somewhere else, and you'd follow that sound anywhere. Now, a forest in autumn, near the river Yamuna.

The cowherd boys are driving the cows out to graze, and one of them lifts a bamboo flute to his lips. In the village, the young women called the gopis hear it. And according to the Bhagavata, so does everything else.

teach.b: This chapter of the Bhagavata Purana is called the song of the flute, and it's told almost entirely through the gopis, talking to each other about what the music does.
The cows stop grazing, grass still in their mouths. The calves stop drinking their mothers' milk. The deer come out of the woods and stand still.
The birds settle on the branches and close their eyes, as if listening in meditation. Even the rivers, the gopis say, show their feeling: they swirl, and slow, and offer lotus flowers at his feet.
Then the gopis say something surprising. They're jealous of the flute.

teach.h: THE GOPIS ENVY A PIECE OF BAMBOO.
teach.b: What did this piece of bamboo do, they ask, to drink the nectar of his lips so often, when we can't? Here's what devotees have heard in that jealousy for centuries.
The flute is a plain thing, a hollow stick with nothing inside. Many teachers say that's exactly why Krishna plays it. It's empty, so the breath passes through it and becomes music.
The dream is to become hollow enough to be played. That reading isn't in the verses; it's what generations of devotees have drawn from them.
And it names the heart of bhakti, devotion: what stands in the way isn't a lack of talent, it's the ego, the part of us that wants the credit.

teach.h: EMPTY OF EGO, SO GOD CAN PLAY.
teach.b: Empty that out, and God can play through you.
It's why, when devotees sing to Krishna, the aim isn't to sound impressive. The song is his breath. You're the bamboo.

how: Krishna is almost always shown with his flute, and devotees sing the gopis' songs from the Bhagavata; in many traditions the flute is taught as a picture of the devotee, empty of ego so God can play through them.

o: action, even just letting the breath through
the songs devotees sing to Krishna at night
a gift you earn by being good enough

games.q: the song of the flute — tap the pairs.
p: stopped with grass in their mouths
hollow, so the breath becomes music

s: in the Bhagavata, only people hear Krishna's flute
cows, calves, deer, birds and even rivers respond to it.
the gopis say they're jealous of the flute
it gets to touch his lips so often, and they can't.
the 'hollow flute' reading is written in the verses
it's a reading generations of devotees have drawn from them.

games.q: you're one of the gopis, hearing the flute from the village. who do you find yourself envying?
games.why: the gopis envy a piece of bamboo, because it gets so close to him. devotees hear in it the wish to be hollow enough to be played.

practice: Sit comfortably and softly say or hum Krishna's name, or just the sound om, and let the breath carry it out like air through bamboo.
When a thought snags, a worry, a plan, a wish to sound good, notice it and let the next breath carry it through; you don't have to make music, just stay open. If you pray, you can ask to be played.

wordCard.voice: Karma, action, is the word these weeks carry. In the song of the flute, the only action is letting the breath through, and the whole forest listens.

orig.note: Sanskrit: bamboo, and a bamboo flute. Bhagavata 10.21 is known as the Venu Gita, the song of the flute.

carryVoice: Your line: empty of ego, so God can play through you. The music was never the bamboo's. Day three hundred nine.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 10.21 (the Venu Gita, the song of the flute)
